name: Primary CNS lymphoma
aliases: primary diffuse large B-cell lymphoma of the CNS
CD20+ MYD88-mutated CNS large B-cell lymphoma

clinicalPearls: An aggressive extranodal lymphoma confined to the brain, spinal cord, leptomeninges, or eyes without systemic disease at diagnosis
Presents with focal neurological deficits, cognitive or personality change, raised intracranial pressure, or seizures, and around a fifth have ocular involvement
Most cases are diffuse large B-cell lymphomas, frequently harbouring MYD88 and CD79B mutations
In immunocompetent patients tumours are usually Epstein-Barr virus-negative, whereas immunodeficiency-associated (e.g. HIV or post-transplant) cases are typically EBV-driven
Imaging characteristically shows homogeneously enhancing periventricular lesions that are markedly diffusion-restricting
Corticosteroids can rapidly shrink lesions and obscure histology, so biopsy should ideally precede steroids where safe

Treatment centres on high-dose methotrexate-based combination chemotherapy, often with rituximab, sometimes consolidated by autologous transplantation, with radiotherapy used selectively because of neurotoxicity
reference.pathophysiology: Primary central nervous system lymphoma is an aggressive B-cell neoplasm, usually of diffuse large B-cell type, that arises within and remains confined to the central nervous system and eyes. The malignant cells are typically of activated B-cell origin and characteristically carry mutations activating B-cell receptor and toll-like receptor signalling, such as MYD88 and CD79B. Tumour cells cluster around blood vessels within the brain parenchyma, and how the clone becomes restricted to this immune-privileged site remains incompletely understood. In immunodeficient hosts, impaired surveillance allows Epstein-Barr virus to drive transformation, accounting for the EBV positivity seen in that setting.
additionalDifferentials: Demyelinating disease such as a tumefactive multiple sclerosis lesion
Neurosarcoidosis or other inflammatory CNS disease
Secondary CNS involvement by systemic lymphoma
additionalInvestigations: Contrast-enhanced MRI of the brain and whole neuraxis
Stereotactic brain biopsy (ideally before corticosteroids) with immunohistochemistry
Cerebrospinal fluid cytology and flow cytometry, with clonality studies
Slit-lamp examination and vitreous sampling to assess ocular involvement
HIV testing and EBV studies on tissue or cerebrospinal fluid
Systemic staging (PET-CT, bone marrow, and in men testicular assessment) to confirm disease is CNS-limited
redFlags: Rapidly rising intracranial pressure or impending herniation
Progressive obtundation or new focal deficits
Leptomeningeal or ocular dissemination requiring additional directed therapy
reference.prognosis: Untreated disease is rapidly fatal, but high-dose methotrexate-based regimens achieve remission in many patients; older age, poor performance status, and treatment-related neurotoxicity limit long-term outcomes, and relapse is common.
pitfalls: Giving corticosteroids before biopsy, which can transiently dissolve the tumour and render histology non-diagnostic
Mistaking lesions for glioma, demyelination, or, in HIV, toxoplasmosis
Failing to examine the eyes and cerebrospinal fluid for occult involvement
Omitting systemic staging and thereby misclassifying secondary CNS lymphoma as primary
references: Swerdlow SH et al. WHO monograph on lymphoid neoplasms
management: Avoid corticosteroids before biopsy where possible since steroids can shrink the tumour and obscure histopathologic diagnosis, unless mass effect or impending herniation requires urgent treatment
Diagnose via stereotactic brain biopsy, using CSF molecular markers only to raise suspicion when the lesion is not surgically accessible

Stage with brain MRI, CSF cytology and flow cytometry, slit-lamp ophthalmologic evaluation, and systemic imaging plus testicular ultrasound in men and bone marrow evaluation to exclude disease outside the CNS
Assess baseline fitness, cognition, and organ function before selecting treatment
Reserve surgery for diagnostic biopsy or for debulking large lesions causing acute mass effect, since routine resection has no established survival benefit and carries neurologic risk

Triage patients by fitness into three groups, those fit for intensive immunochemotherapy with transplant consolidation, those fit only for high-dose methotrexate-based immunochemotherapy without transplant, and those fit only for palliative care

Base induction in fit patients on high-dose methotrexate, typically combined with cytarabine, an alkylating agent, and or an anti-CD20 monoclonal antibody, recognising that rituximab's benefit is supported by mixed evidence rather than uniformly proven

After induction response in fit patients, consolidate with high-dose chemotherapy and autologous stem-cell transplant or reduced-dose whole-brain radiotherapy, favouring transplant-based approaches where feasible for better cognitive preservation, and deferring radiotherapy to relapse when an active nontransplant consolidation is used instead

In elderly or less fit patients, use methotrexate-based induction when organ function and fitness allow, favour oral alkylating agents combined with methotrexate, defer whole-brain radiotherapy to relapse given higher neurotoxicity risk, and consider maintenance therapy after response
Reserve transplant-based consolidation in older patients for carefully selected fit individuals up to around age 70
Avoid focal radiation or radiosurgery given the infiltrative, often multifocal nature of the disease, and reserve whole-brain radiotherapy alone for patients unfit for chemotherapy
Manage ocular involvement, present in roughly a fifth of patients, with intravitreal chemotherapy or ocular radiotherapy

Perform regular surveillance neuroimaging after treatment given the frequency of relapse, and assess response using the disease's dedicated criteria combining imaging, corticosteroid dose, ophthalmologic findings, and CSF cytology

For relapsed or refractory disease, prioritise clinical trial enrollment, and otherwise consider rechallenge with methotrexate-based therapy, transplant in previously untransplanted fit patients, or whole-brain radiotherapy in patients who have not yet received it, while managing suspected or confirmed cases within a combined haemato-oncology and neuro-oncology multidisciplinary team from diagnosis

nodes.text: Suspected primary CNS lymphoma: progressive focal or encephalopathic brain disease
Raised intracranial pressure, obtundation, status epilepticus or ocular spread?
Escalate: urgent neurosurgical and oncology review for raised pressure
Contrast MRI of brain and neuraxis; CSF cytology; systemic staging
Does stereotactic biopsy confirm lymphoma with CNS-limited disease?
Consider glioma, toxoplasmosis or metastasis; repeat diagnostic biopsy
Assess fitness, cognition and organ function to select therapy
Fit: high-dose methotrexate with cytarabine, then consolidation
Less fit: methotrexate-based induction or oral alkylating agents
Surveillance imaging after treatment; trials or rechallenge for relapse
